title: Ouilets: Little Apps for Deciding Together
summary: Built a family of small, no-account apps for deciding things together from your phones: what to watch, where to eat, and who is winning. Three apps in one monorepo, shipped to the web and submitted to both app stores.

challenge.p: Picking a movie with my family always turned into the same argument: endless scrolling, nobody willing to commit, and no one remembering which streaming services we actually pay for. Picking a restaurant was worse, because everyone says "I don't mind." Keeping score at the kitchen table ended with someone disputing a number. I wanted a tiny app for each of these, usable from a phone, with no sign up.

Each app on its own is small. The interesting problem was building the second and third without copying the first, and without turning a weekend project into the kind of micro-frontend platform I build at work. The constraints I set for the whole family of apps were:

ul: No accounts. A device token tied to a chosen name and a four-letter join code is the entire identity model.
Nothing is kept for long. Parties expire after seven days, and the app never plays video or serves food. It only helps the group decide.
Free-tier hosting only, so every design choice had to fit within Vercel Hobby, Render free, and MongoDB Atlas M0.
A structure I could add to in an evening, with gates that keep the code tidy when I am moving fast.

solution.p: I set the project up as one Bun workspaces monorepo with a small app contract. Each ouilet exports an OuiApp object (base path, brand, root component), and the web shell lazy-loads it and sets the brand on the document. That gave me a micro-frontend-ready seam without any federation, which I recorded in the first ADR.

solution.alt: Oui! Let's... on iPhone: the launcher, a Watch Together lobby with party code and streaming services, a swipe card, a match, and the decided screen.

ul: A shared party engine that owns the lobby, join codes, presence, and phase state over one Socket.IO room per party. It has a headless entry point so the web and native apps share the same engine, and a test fails the build if anything other than react, socket.io-client, and the shared package leaks into it.

Watch Together: swipe-to-match against the TMDB catalog, filtered to the services the group actually has. Lobby events use a load, reduce, save loop with optimistic concurrency. Swipes use a single atomic, idempotent update so five people swiping at once cannot cause a retry storm. Matches are re-checked against live streaming availability before they are announced.
Eat Together: Google Places text search with three-bucket preferences and hard quota caps so a busy night cannot run up a bill.
Keep Score: an entered score stays pending until another player approves it, and the server rejects self-approval.
Multi-brand theming from one stylesheet. The three brands differ by hue only, scoped by a data-brand attribute, with a parity test in CI.
A native host built with Expo and React Native. It runs Watch Together natively, opens the other ouilets in-app, and uses design tokens generated from the same brand CSS.
A structure doctrine enforced by four custom gates in CI and pre-commit: hub-and-spoke layout, one component per file, import layers checked with dependency-cruiser, and brand parity.
Live at ouilets.com with three apps, six shared packages, and one API, built in about five weeks across 293 commits.
1,058 tests across the web, native, and API code, running in one CI job alongside the structure gates.
Submitted to both app stores. The Android build is installed and working on my own phone through Play internal testing, and the iOS build is in App Review.
Runs at zero fixed cost. The only monetisation is affiliate links where a link already existed, plus a one-off Supporter purchase through Stripe that is verified server-side.
Seven ADRs and thirteen design specs mean the next ouilet is one OuiApp export and a shell route, not a new repo.

title: GlobalJam: Remote Rehearsal for Bands
summary: Built a platform for bands split across cities and countries to rehearse together and come away with time-aligned, multi-track recordings. A React micro-frontend host, fourteen Go services, and a native Rust audio bridge, shipped to production and then rebuilt to run at zero hosting cost.

challenge.p: I play in a band with members in Auckland and Gainesville, Florida, about 13,000 km apart. Playing together in real time breaks down above roughly 25 ms of one-way latency, intercontinental round trips sit near 200 ms, and browsers add another 20 to 100 ms of audio overhead on top. There is no engineering around that.
So I had to decide what was honestly possible and what musicians would actually pay for. That meant solving:

ul: Audio has to leave the browser. Direct device access, Opus with forward error correction, and an adaptive jitter buffer are a native problem.
Every musician needs a shared clock and a shared click, so that whatever they hear live, the recording lines up sample-accurately.
Peer-to-peer UDP fails behind many home and campus networks, so the audio path needs its own relay.
My first production footprint on Kubernetes cost low hundreds of dollars a month with zero users. The platform had to survive long enough to find them.

solution.alt: GlobalJam web app: sign in, the welcome walkthrough, the Audio Bridge setup step, the rooms list, inside a room waiting for bandmates, and session history.

solution.p: I built the platform in three parts: a web app for bands, rooms, and sessions; a set of Go services behind one gateway; and a native Audio Bridge that handles the audio the browser cannot. Key pieces of the solution:

ul: The Audio Bridge, written in Rust: CPAL device I/O, Opus at 48 kHz in 20 ms frames with in-band FEC, UDP peer-to-peer transport, a 5 to 40 ms adaptive jitter buffer, dropout detection, and a soft-knee master limiter. I signed and notarised the macOS builds, and the same workflow produces Windows and Linux builds.

Tempo-Lock: NTP-style clock sync over UDP to sub-millisecond offsets, a shared click at the session tempo, and onset detection. Every stream is timestamped, and sessions render as time-aligned 24-bit FLAC stems plus a click stem.
Two-plane audio. Talk-back voice rides WebRTC with echo cancellation and noise suppression; performance audio never touches it.

Per-pair routing chosen from measured round-trip time: direct UDP under 25 ms, Tempo-Lock above it, and a TURN relay built into the bridge when UDP is blocked, using ephemeral HMAC credentials and peer attribution keyed on channel number rather than packet source.

A React 19 micro-frontend host on Rspack and Module Federation with ten feature plugins (rooms, sessions, bands, audio bridge, video, livestream, and more), backed by fourteen Go services behind a routes-driven gateway with JWT, RBAC, and a Redis-backed WebSocket hub.

When the hosting bill became the problem, I composed the thirteen Kubernetes deployments into one Go binary through per-service build packages and moved it to Render, Neon Postgres, Backblaze B2, and an Oracle Always Free VM for TURN. No rewrite, and every existing test still runs.
I documented the design in twelve ADRs, and ran the implementation waves with a crew of 31 repo-scoped AI agents and 18 skills working in parallel git worktrees.
Shipped to production at global-jams.com through v1.0.10 with a three-stage promotion pipeline (test, release candidate, production) on byte-identical images.
948 commits in six months, with 2,517 Go tests, 919 Rust tests, and 3,444 frontend test cases, plus Playwright end-to-end coverage.
Monthly hosting cost went from low hundreds of dollars to zero with no feature loss.
The honest latency model changed the product. GlobalJam now sells remote rehearsal with every part captured as a stem rather than live jamming, and that is the MVP I am validating with outside bands.
